claims.explanation: Bergenin's anti-inflammatory activity, including inhibition of IL-1β and TNF-α, likely sensitizes cancer cells that depend on autocrine or paracrine IL-1/TNF signaling for survival. Lines with high expression of IL1B, TNF, or their receptors, or with mutations that activate NF-κB (e.g., in NFKBIA, TRAF3, or MYD88), may be more responsive to this inhibition, while those with low inflammatory signaling or protective mutations in the pathway are less affected.

features.basis: Bergenin is annotated as an interleukin inhibitor targeting IL1B; high expression may indicate dependence on IL-1β signaling.
Bergenin targets TNF and inhibits its production; high expression may indicate reliance on TNF for survival.
Damaging mutations in NFKBIA can lead to constitutive NF-κB activation, which may increase dependence on inflammatory cytokines that bergenin inhibits.
Loss-of-function mutations in TRAF3 can activate non-canonical NF-κB signaling, potentially sensitizing to anti-inflammatory agents.
Activating MYD88 mutations drive NF-κB and inflammatory cytokine production, which bergenin may counteract.
High expression of the IL-1 receptor may enhance sensitivity to IL-1 signaling inhibition by bergenin.
High expression of TNF receptor 1 may increase dependence on TNF signaling, which bergenin inhibits.
Low expression of NF-κB subunits may reduce inflammatory signaling and decrease sensitivity to bergenin.
Low expression of RELA (p65) may diminish NF-κB-mediated survival signals, reducing the impact of bergenin.
Bergenin acts as a PPARγ agonist; high PPARγ expression may enhance its anti-inflammatory and anti-survival effects.
Bergenin improves SIRT1 expression, which inhibits NF-κB; high SIRT1 may potentiate bergenin's effects.
Damaging KEAP1 mutations activate Nrf2, which may protect against oxidative stress and reduce bergenin's efficacy.
